summary: Specifies a format for transporting and provisioning symmetric keys, such as one-time password shared secrets, to cryptographic modules like authentication devices. A common format lets different vendors' components work together.

eli5.summary: Little security gadgets need secret numbers loaded in them. This is a standard envelope for those secrets so any maker's tools can load them.

questions: what is a portable symmetric key container
how are otp keys provisioned to tokens
subtitle: A standard XML envelope for moving secret keys, such as one-time-password seeds, between vendors' systems and devices.

tldr.problem: Vendors of authentication servers and tokens used proprietary formats to import and export symmetric keys, which made it hard to mix tokens and systems from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: PSKC defines an XML key container that carries keys plus metadata such as device, algorithm, counter and usage policy, and can encrypt the key values, add a MAC and sign the whole document.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6030 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It also creates IANA registries for algorithm profiles, versions and key usages.

today: RFC 6030 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the PSKC format it introduced.

sections.title: Why a Key Container
sections.content:
Systems that use symmetric keys, for example for strong authentication with One-Time Password (OTP) and Challenge/Response (CR) mechanisms, need a way to import and export (provision) those keys. Traditionally, vendors of authentication servers and service providers used proprietary formats, so it was hard to use tokens from two different vendors.

RFC 6030 defines the Portable Symmetric Key Container (PSKC), an XML-based container for symmetric keys and key-related metadata. It also specifies the information needed when a key is used for a specific purpose, such as the initial counter for the HMAC-Based One-Time Password (HOTP) algorithm, and it creates an IANA registry for algorithm profiles.

Only version 1.0 is specified. Versions are numbered major.minor, and the two numbers are compared as separate integers, so PSKC 2.4 is lower than PSKC 2.13.
sections.eli5: Every gadget maker used to have their own secret envelope, so the gadgets did not mix. PSKC is one shared envelope everybody agrees on.

sections.title: The Container and Its Entities
sections.content:
A PSKC document is built from a few nested entities. The KeyContainer carries one or more KeyPackage entities; a valid container MUST carry at least one. Each KeyPackage holds at most one key and its endpoint: an optional DeviceInfo (the physical or virtual device) and an optional CryptoModuleInfo (the module where the key lives or goes).

The Key entity represents the key itself. Its Data entity is a list of metadata items such as Secret and Counter. Each item holds its value either in plaintext (PlainValue) or encrypted (EncryptedValue, with an optional ValueMAC).

The document marks mandatory elements and attributes; anything not marked as mandatory is optional.
sections.eli5: Think of a box (the container) holding folders (packages). Each folder has a note about the gadget and, at most, one secret key with a few labelled facts.

sections.title: Keys, Devices and Parameters
sections.content:
A Key MUST carry an Id (an alphanumeric string that stays the same across containers that refer to the same key) and an Algorithm (the URI of an algorithm profile). Optional children include Issuer, FriendlyName and AlgorithmParameters. Under Data the RFC defines Secret, Counter, Time, TimeInterval and TimeDrift.

Secret values are base64-encoded octet strings. Unless an algorithm says otherwise, they follow the AES key value encoding, where the first octet becomes key byte 0. The RFC gives test values for AES and for Triple DES key bundles.

DeviceInfo identifies the device with elements such as Manufacturer, SerialNo, Model, IssueNo and DeviceBinding. A Manufacturer value MUST come from the OATH prefixes (prefixed with oath.) or from the IANA Private Enterprise Numbers (prefixed with iana.). UserId is informational only.

AlgorithmParameters can hold Suite, ChallengeFormat and ResponseFormat. The encodings are DECIMAL, HEXADECIMAL, ALPHANUMERIC, BASE64 and BINARY, and a Luhn check digit can be used with DECIMAL.

For key derivation schemes, KeyProfileId names a set of key attribute values agreed out of band, and KeyReference points to an external master key (such as a PKCS #11 key label). In that case the Key carries no Secret.
sections.eli5: Each key has a name tag, a note saying which kind of code maker it feeds, and the numbers it needs, such as how many codes were already used. The folder also says which gadget it belongs to.

sections.title: Key Policy and PINs
sections.content:
The Policy element attaches rules to a key. If a recipient does not understand something in a Policy, it MUST assume the key may not be used, so unknown extensions cannot lead to unintended use.

Policy children include StartDate and ExpiryDate (the key may only be used between them, inclusive), NumberOfTransactions (a maximum number of uses; no limit when omitted), KeyUsage and PINPolicy. The recipient MUST enforce KeyUsage, which can be repeated; when absent, any usage is allowed.

PINPolicy links a key to a PIN stored as another key (via PINKeyId) and sets how the PIN is used through PINUsageMode: Local (checked on the device), Prepend or Append (added to the response and checked by the validating party), or Algorithmic (part of the computation). It also has MaxFailedAttempts, MinLength, MaxLength and PINEncoding. For Local mode the device MUST enforce the limits; otherwise the server does.

The PIN algorithm is a straight octet comparison: it matches only if both values have the same octet length and all octets are equal.
sections.eli5: The policy is a list of rules stuck on the key: use it only this month, only for making codes, and only if the right PIN is typed. If the rule is written in a language the reader does not know, the key stays locked.

sections.title: Protecting Keys in Transit
sections.content:
Without protection, keys travel in cleartext. The EncryptionKey element, a child of KeyContainer, lets the sender encrypt the value of individual elements, and the same encryption algorithm MUST be used for all encrypted elements. If the algorithm uses an initialization vector, a random one MUST be generated for each value and prepended to the encrypted value.

Three methods are defined:

  • Pre-shared keys: the key is named in KeyName. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to support AES-128-CBC and KW-AES128. Because AES-128-CBC has no integrity check, a keyed MAC goes in ValueMAC and the MACMethod is declared; HMAC-SHA1 is RECOMMENDED, and the sender is RECOMMENDED to generate a random MAC key and encrypt it with the same encryption key.
  • Passphrase-based keys: the XML Encryption 1.1 DerivedKey element MUST be used, with PBKDF2 parameters such as salt and iteration count.
  • Asymmetric keys: the certificate is given in X509Data and the algorithm in EncryptionMethod. The RFC recommends implementing RSA-1.5.

When the cipher needs padded input, PKCS #5 padding is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Before mailing the secret you can lock it in a box. The key to the box can be one you both already know, a password you both type in, or a lock that only the receiver can open.

sections.title: Signatures and Bulk Provisioning
sections.content:
A digital signature, as defined by XML Signature, can be added as a child of KeyContainer. It gives integrity and authenticity that survive after the container has left its transport channel.

Bulk provisioning needs no extra mechanism: the KeyPackage element is simply repeated, and one EncryptionKey applies to all packages. To give one device several keys, repeat the package with a DeviceInfo that has the same identifying sub-elements.

PSKC also defines algorithm profiles in Section 10. The HOTP profile requires ResponseFormat and Counter, key material of at least 16 octets (128 bits) if a Secret is present, DECIMAL encoding, and a length from 6 to 9. The PIN profile requires the Secret.
sections.eli5: You can stamp the whole envelope with a seal so the receiver knows it is real and untouched. To send lots of gadgets at once, you just put many folders in the same box.

sections.title: Registries and Media Type
sections.content:
RFC 6030 registers the media type application/pskc+xml (file extension .pskcxml), the XML schema and a URN sub-namespace.

It also creates three IANA registries. The PSKC Algorithm Profile registry records each profile's common name, class, URI, definitions, contact and a deprecated flag; it has two initial entries, HOTP and PIN, and requires Specification Required. The PSKC Version registry starts with 1.0, and new versions need standards action. The Key Usage registry starts with the eleven tokens from Section 5 and requires Specification Required with expert review.

Section 9 lists the extension points: new versions, new elements and attributes, new algorithm profiles, new algorithm URIs and policy values.
sections.eli5: A public list keeps track of the allowed kinds of secrets and rules, so new ones can be added without anyone's envelope getting confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PSKC document carries sensitive keys and may cross from one secure perimeter to another, so confidentiality, integrity and authenticity MUST be ensured.

For confidentiality there are two approaches. The key data can be encrypted, in which case no transport layer security is required. Or lower-layer mechanisms such as TLS or IPsec can protect it, in which case the endpoints must be authenticated to rule out man-in-the-middle attacks. Passphrase-based encryption is open to password dictionary attacks, so strong passwords apply, and implementations are strongly RECOMMENDED to use a salt and an iteration count, with a different salt per PSKC.

For integrity and authenticity, the digital signature is the main tool, and it is RECOMMENDED to sign the entire container. TLS or IPsec can also give authenticity, but nothing can be verified once the container has been delivered, which makes that weaker than a signature.
sections.eli5: The secrets are valuable, so either lock them in a box or send them down a guarded tunnel, and make sure you are talking to the right person. A seal on the envelope proves nobody changed it.

children.label: Key
children.note: 0..1; has Id, Algorithm, Policy and Data (Secret, Counter, ...)

items.label: Integrity
items.desc: Only to generate a keyed message digest.

items.label: Verify
items.desc: Only to verify a keyed message digest.

items.label: Unlock
items.desc: Only for inverse Challenge/Response after a device lock caused by wrong PINs.

items.label: Derive
items.desc: Only with a key derivation function.

items.label: Generate
items.desc: Only to generate a new key from a random number and the previous key.

cells: AES-128-CBC and KW-AES128 recommended; MAC needed for AES-128-CBC
